posts.body:
JaoRPG – Just another Role-Playing-Game
​
A quirky, story-rich RPG about self-discovery, nature, and the bond between player and protagonist.
---
Synopsis
Sarah is an ordinary young woman – she goes to work on the farm, follows her daily routine, and rarely questions the world around her. But one day, she follows the call of the mist… and steps into another world.
There she realizes she is more than she ever imagined. Strange voices echo in her head – the player’s voice – guiding her through choices big and small. Each decision shapes her personality, revealing who Sarah truly is.
On her journey, she encounters Frederick – a talkative, knowledge-hungry cleric with a tendency to overshare. Though not the main hero, he adds color (and a lot of words) to Sarah’s path, sometimes helping, sometimes just making her sigh.
Between life and death, she explores a transformed nature: a world where evolution has taken its own path, where even leaves can become deadly if balance demands it.
At its core, JaoRPG is a story about self-discovery and the bond between player and protagonist, wrapped in a journey through a wild, shifting world that struggles to find harmony again.
---
Current Progress
• Chapter 1 completed
• First miniboss implemented
• Multilanguage support (German, English, Spanish, French, and a fun “Elvish” mode )
• More chapters and features planned
---
Play online / Demo
Play JaoRPG on Itch.io
---
Media
---
Feedback
This is still a WIP project – feedback of any kind is very welcome!
Thanks a lot for taking a look, and I hope you’ll enjoy exploring JaoRPG.

posts.author: hiddenone
posts.body:
Heyas, I gave your demo a try and stopped after meeting Frederick because I couldn't find a new area to explore. It seems like you have a lot of ideas for this project, but I think it's suffering from a lack of focus at the moment.
Spoiler:
Feedback
I didn't get to experience much of the story, so I won't comment on it. I do need to talk about the translation though, since I was playing the English version and a lot of German was left scattered throughout the menus and even in some of the cutscenes. The Leaf's battle tutorial, for example, was entirely in German so if I wasn't already familiar with RPGs I would have had no clue what I was supposed to do. Having other options for languages is a lovely idea, but only if they help the player actually understand the game.
I was a bit confused by the graphic styles in this game. Character sprites are Time Fantasy which is a great choice for an RPG, but the tiles are a mishmash of other styles. Using the below screenshot of the forest as an example, there are at least three different art styles on a single map! While mixing styles
can
work, it needs to be done with intention. Right now it feels more like you are using placeholders without a plan, which makes the game feel thrown together. You're using the Time Fantasy sprites, so why not use the tilesets too? The passability of the tiles also made it hard to navigate, since I couldn't go behind most trees so it felt like you didn't want me to explore the game world. I was better off sticking to the path and not even trying to look around.
Battles are where I think this game really suffers. I did not find the miniboss you mentioned, so all I could fight were Leaves and a few Plants. None of the enemies posed a threat, so I ended up just spamming Attack or Double Strike whenever I was in a fight. The battles felt like you added them just because an RPG should have them, not because they added to the experience. I think it would be good if you took some time to decide if you want battles in the game or not, since I think you could get away with having a battle-free game based on what I played. You described Sarah as an ordinary woman so it would make sense for her to not be able to fight well, and that could lead to a bunch of interesting puzzles or quests to help her survive her world without battling every little Leaf that gets in her way.
The Quest Journal also let me down. I found my way to the farm but there wasn't a cutscene or message about what I was supposed to be doing, so I was wandering around collecting things randomly. I spoke to the farmer just because he was there, so imagine my surprise when he started talking about a list of tasks! I checked the Journal and it had updated, but I hadn't been told. If the player needs to keep track of things with the Journal, then they need to know when it updates.
I ended up stopping after I met Frederick (whose dialogue went offscreen a few times), since I couldn't find anywhere else to go and the Journal didn't add a new quest. I assume that's the end of the demo, but there wasn't any obvious message so I can't know for sure.
There were a few other bugs and oddities:
MC stands on bookshelf when hitting switch in her home
The intro chest just says "[intro.chest1]"
Failure in the Quest Journal to properly display names
The Anchovy picture is off to the side instead of in the middle of the screen, which makes it almost look like the Anchovy is speaking
Can walk onto the fronts of all the houses besides Sarah's
Have to click to activate the map transfer from the flower field above the town, which isn't needed to get there. Could leave players confused as to why they can't go back
The default Staff swings behind Sarah's battler sprite, so it looks like there are two staves at once
The crafting tutorial words are cut off, making it hard to tell what exactly it means
The Farmer event is broken, so I can repeatedly 'finish' the quest and get 250 exp and 5 Pumpkins. This means I can level up well beyond what I bet the game wants
Game said I learned Triple Strike at level 10, but it's not actually available
And lastly, a few minor gripes I had while playing. These are all subjective so whether or not you want to make any of these changes is all up to you and what you want out of your project.
Spoiler
The tile passabilities are all strange, I can walk behind some bookcases but not others, and I can't walk behind the brown trees near the fishing pond. It would be good to go through and fix all the passabilities so it's easier for players to move around the maps
The fishing results don't need to have two message windows, you could include the messages all in one
Fishing can be done forever, so Sarah has unlimited funds. Is that on purpose?
There's no response after making a decision with the guy who lost money, so Friendliness doesn't feel like a real thing. Would be better to have him respond in some way after it
Why are there both random encounters and on-map enemies? It would make more sense for there to only be one or the other, not both on the same map when it doesn't happen anywhere else
Overall, I can tell that this is a very early build, so luckily you can start fixing things before getting too far into development. I think taking some time to decide whether you want this to be a combat-heavy game or not would be good, since right now the battles felt like an afterthought and the focus was on interacting with the game world. There are a lot of paths this game could take, so I hope you find one that really showcases the story you want to tell.
Good luck with your project!

Hi, and thank you so much for your very detailed feedback.
First off – without making excuses – you’re right: I’m probably not the most focused dev, and when I went on holiday I kind of panicked and just wanted to finally release something. Mostly to see if I’m making this game just for myself or if there are still people out there who share the old RPG passion. That’s how I stumbled into this forum, actually.
So I’m really glad you took the time to test it so thoroughly. That motivates me to keep working on it. Early tests with people close to me showed that the little battle scenes were already too difficult, so I tuned them way down. Battles are meant to be part of the game, but there will also be puzzles and quests to balance things.
Some of the language bugs you mentioned I had already noticed, and I absolutely need to pay more attention to how long a translated message can get once it’s switched. That’s one reason I hoped other people would try different languages and point me straight to those mistakes.
I’ll prioritize fixing untranslated cutscenes like the Leaf tutorial, since that’s critical for non-German players.
Maybe, after my next chapter, I'll upgrade my Plugin to find gap's in translation and window leaving parts.
I’m a bit of a “busy bee” who gets lost in details, then wakes up and realizes: “Hey, you actually need to move forward!” That’s probably why there are half-finished features and mismatched tilesets in the demo. I’ll keep an eye on this and try to balance things better.
About the art style: honestly, to me it already felt kind of fitting. But clearly I still need more practice in looking at it with “player’s eyes” instead of “dev eyes.” I’ll keep working on making the maps more consistent.
Before RPG Maker I experimented with my own Java implementations, but I noticed I was spending more time building features than actually telling the story. That’s why I’m happy RPG Maker has so much ready to use – even if I still struggle to tie it all together. And yes, story writing is definitely my weak spot. I’m currently working on Chapter 2, and it’s not easy to connect my wife’s short stories into a coherent whole. I’m a pretty bad storyteller on my own, so I need a lot of time to piece things together in detail.
Once again, thank you for pushing through my messy prototype.
About you not finding the end: I definitely hid it too well – sorry! I was remembering games like Vampires Dawn or other old browser RPGs where you had to wander and search in what felt like disconnected worlds, and I thought that was cool.
The miniboss is on the map before the farm – once Frederick joins, you have to find the two switches.
He really exists – here’s proof:
After that, on the map with the mountain lake, there’s another hidden spot (at the edge of the map) with the hint about where Chapter 2 continues. I’ll patch this better next time – especially with clearer Quest Journal entries and more information. I didn’t want it to feel “too much” and ended up cutting too much instead.
The Quest Journal system clearly needs more polish – I’ll make sure it gives visible updates when entries change.
About the battles: they were deliberately toned down for the demo. Since the story isn’t very far yet, I wanted combat to start simple and grow step by step – with stronger bosses and an elemental system adding more depth later. (I admit, I love dealing big flashy skill damage
).
I did consider making the game battle-free, but in the end I feel battles should be part of the journey – not the main focus, but another layer alongside the story and puzzles. They also reflect the theme: nature itself should feel dangerous and overwhelming if you don’t pay attention. Sarah will grow into her role over time, and it won’t always be just harmless little leaves coming after her…
All the smaller bugs you pointed out I’ll check right away – like getting Sarah off that bookshelf (that switch event keeps haunting me, every time I think I’ve fixed it, it comes back
). And Harvey the farmer shouldn’t be handing out unlimited EXP and pumpkins either – cheeky guy slipped through my testing.
All in all: thank you again for your super detailed and critical feedback without being provocative or aggressive. I love your constructive tone and I really hope I can keep you interested as a critic for Chapter 2.
(spoilers are coming soon
)

Make sure you take a step back now and then to make sure everything is working together as intended. If you're a 'busy bee' then the game is like your 'hive', so you should know what the end results should be (even if it's vague) and keep in mind that expanding isn't the only thing that can be done. Building on what you have already made and making sure it's sturdy is even more important than adding new things to your project.
Nusseysen said:
About the art style: honestly, to me it already felt kind of fitting. But clearly I still need more practice in looking at it with “player’s eyes” instead of “dev eyes.” I’ll keep working on making the maps more consistent.
Click to expand...
If you want Sarah to look like she doesn't belong in the world, then mixing styles can work but it does need to be done with care. A pretty good way to get people to stop and look at your project is to have pretty maps, so it's worth it to make sure your tiles look consistent and your maps strike a balance between looking good and making it enjoyable to explore.
Nusseysen said:
About you not finding the end: I definitely hid it too well – sorry! I was remembering games like Vampires Dawn or other old browser RPGs where you had to wander and search in what felt like disconnected worlds, and I thought that was cool.
The miniboss is on the map before the farm – once Frederick joins, you have to find the two switches.
Click to expand...
Oh, so Frederick has to be in the party? That's where I went wrong, I found both the switches on my way to the farm before meeting him. I hit them both but nothing happened, so it seemed like that hadn't be implemented yet. It would be good to make that clearer, either by having the switches require some magic from Frederick to activate them or have the miniboss spawn when it's just Sarah and have Sarah comment on not wanting to try to fight it by herself.
Nusseysen said:
After that, on the map with the mountain lake, there’s another hidden spot (at the edge of the map) with the hint about where Chapter 2 continues. I’ll patch this better next time – especially with clearer Quest Journal entries and more information. I didn’t want it to feel “too much” and ended up cutting too much instead.
Click to expand...
Hidden locations can make players explore, but there needs to be a reward for it. I searched the first forest map and didn't find anything but some Leaf battles, so I didn't bother looking around the second forest map since it seemed empty at first glance.
You mentioned taking inspiration from older games, and I think you should take the mechanics in those games with a grain of salt. Nowadays a game needs to draw the player in to make them want to spend more time searching and finding the game's secrets, while older games could get away with not sharing details since there were fewer games to choose from (and even then, think about how annoying some games like King's Quest could be when it comes to figuring out what to do next!). I haven't played Vampire's Dawn before, but I'm guessing that it had a focused intro that got people to care about the characters or gameplay right away before throwing in seemingly disconnected worlds.
Nusseysen said:
About the battles: they were deliberately toned down for the demo. Since the story isn’t very far yet, I wanted combat to start simple and grow step by step – with stronger bosses and an elemental system adding more depth later.
Click to expand...
I understand why you would think that way, but I think that's actually a terrible way to go about combat. You want to give people a taste of what they can expect later, not just have a default rpg system! What makes your combat system fun? What makes people want to keep battling foes? The battles don't all need to be long and challenging, but there should be something that makes the player feel like it's worthwhile to fight (Exp and money just don't cut it).
If an elemental system is going to be important in the game, then introduce it right away. Give Sarah two weak elemental skills, one that is effective against Leaves and one that isn't, and let your players learn that using the right skill against the right enemy will make battles a lot more quick and enjoyable. Then you could introduce another enemy that has the opposite elemental weakness as the Leaf, teaching your players that one method won't work against every enemy. Something like this would still keep early battles straightforward without the battles feeling like spamming Attack is the best strategy.

Wow, thank you again for taking the time to give me such detailed feedback.
I have to admit, as a nervous dev , detailed feedback like this can feel a bit overwhelming at first. But I really appreciate how constructive you were – it helps me see the project with clearer eyes and motivates me to keep improving.
About the “busy bee” / hive comparison – that’s a really good way to put it. I’ll try to focus more on polishing what’s already there before adding more features. Expanding is fun, but making the hive sturdy is even more important.
On the art style: to me it already looked kind of fitting, but clearly I need more practice in looking at it with “player’s eyes.” If I want Sarah to feel out of place, I’ll need to do it intentionally. Otherwise, I’ll work on unifying the look and making maps more consistent.
About the miniboss and the switches – that’s super helpful! I didn’t realize players could find both switches before Frederick joins, and then it just feels broken. I’ll definitely fix that by either tying the switches to Frederick’s magic or adding a comment from Sarah if she tries alone. Thanks for pointing that out!
Hidden spots: you’re absolutely right – exploration needs to feel rewarding. If the forest looks empty, players stop searching. I’ll make sure to add more items, lore, or little surprises so wandering off the path feels worthwhile.
And battles – yes, you hit a big point. Just making them “easy now, harder later” isn’t enough. I really like your suggestion about giving Sarah two weak elemental skills right away so players can already taste the elemental system. That would make even simple Leaf fights more interesting. It’s a great idea and I’ll try it out!
All in all – thank you for pushing me with such concrete advice. It helps me see the project with clearer eyes and motivates me to keep improving. I hope you’ll stay curious about Chapter 2, and maybe enjoy testing how I apply your suggestions.
